consensus_summary: Heaven primarily denotes God's transcendent dwelling place, throne, and presence, and derivatively the eternal destiny/home of the redeemed in fellowship with God; common alternatives cover the physical sky/firmament, 'kingdom of heaven' as God's reign, intermediate state of the dead, new-creation union of heaven and earth, and present spiritual sphere.
book_summary: Heaven is the dual shamayim jurisdiction (visible sky and seat of rule) where God's will is already done, set over against earth as the realm delegated to men where His will must still be done; God's motion is downward and the hope is heaven come down, not man gone up.
consensus_core_identification: God's transcendent dwelling/throne and the eternal destiny of the redeemed
book_core_identification: dual sky/rule jurisdiction where God's will is already done (vs. earth), with hope of descent not ascent
boundary_disagreement: Consensus primary includes heaven as the place to which the redeemed go for eternal abode; the book excludes ascent as the hope, reclassifying the eschatological relation as heaven descending to earth and framing the core strictly as the already-obedient jurisdiction.
rationale: Both identify the same central biblical referent (shamayim as God's realm/throne over against earth). The book preserves that category but materially narrows and reorients it around the 'will already done' criterion (Matt 6:10) and the downward vector (Son, city, rain), explicitly rejecting the ascent hope that forms part of the consensus primary 'destiny of the redeemed.' This is boundary disagreement and partial reclassification of eschatological cases already present as alternatives in the consensus (new creation, intermediate vs. final), not replacement of the referent itself; hence REFINED rather than MATCH or DIVERGENT.
strongest_objection: The book's explicit 'not man gone up' could be read as replacing rather than merely narrowing the consensus primary of heaven as the redeemed's eternal home, tipping the relation toward DIVERGENT.
